en: It is also titled *The Collection of Explanations on the Source of Chan*.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Mount Guifeng during the Tang Dynasty,
this *Collection of Explanations on the Source of Chan* transcribes and records the writings of various masters that elucidate the fundamental principles of the Chan school.
The fundamental principles,
along with the words, phrases, and verses,
were compiled into a single collection.
This was done to bequeath [the tradition] to future generations;
thus, this name was inscribed upon the capital.
"Chan" (Dhyāna) is a term from India.
In its full form, it is called *dhyāna*.
In China, it is translated as "contemplative cultivation" (*sīwéixiū*) and is also termed "tranquil reflection" (*jìnglù*).
These are all general designations for meditative concentration and wisdom.
The "source" refers to the fundamentally enlightened true nature of all sentient beings;
it is also called Buddha-nature.
It is also called the "ground of the mind.
Awakening to it is termed wisdom;
cultivating it is termed meditative concentration.
Concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā) are collectively termed dhyāna.
This nature is the fundamental source of dhyāna;
therefore, it is called the "source of dhyāna" (chanyuan).
It is also called "the practice of the principle of dhyāna.
Its fundamental source is the principle of dhyāna;
forgetting the emotions to accord with it is the practice of dhyāna.
Therefore, it is said that there are both principle and practice.
However, among the various works compiled here,
most discuss the principles of Chan while discussing the practice of Chan only sparingly.
Therefore, I have provisionally titled this work *The Source of Chan*.

Nevertheless, it is not that there exists a separate essence of dhyāna apart from the true nature;

If one discusses the fundamental nature directly,

Therefore, it is called the *Tathāgatagarbha* and the *Ālayavijñāna*, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; it is also the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas.
It is likewise called "Buddha-nature" and "Nirvāṇa," as stated in various sūtras; it is also the source of the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas;
this is the root of the bodhisattva path."
This is the root of all the Buddha-sons in the great assembly; the myriad practices do not transcend the six *pāramitās*.
The Chan gate is but one among these six, corresponding to the fifth.
How could one possibly designate the true nature itself as "one practice of dhyāna"?
Nevertheless, the single practice of meditative concentration is most wondrous and subtle;
it is capable of giving rise to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) within that nature.
All sublime functions, the myriad virtues, and the myriad practices,

That which is practiced by those who correctly believe in cause and effect and do so through the cultivation of longing for the pleasant and aversion to the unpleasant is the dhyāna of ordinary worldlings.
Those who practice having realized the principle of the partial truth of self-emptiness (pudgala-śūnyatā) are practitioners of the Śrāvaka vehicle’s dhyāna.
Those who practice having realized the ultimate truth revealed by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (dharma-nairātmya) are [practitioners of the Mahāyāna].
These are the four categories of Mahāyāna dhyāna,

each of which possesses the distinctions of the four form-realm concentrations (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*) and the four formless-realm attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). The nature of untainted wisdom is inherently and spontaneously complete;
this mind is itself the Buddha,
ultimately without any difference.
Those who practice in reliance upon this are practicing the meditation of the Supreme Vehicle;
it is also called the Tathāgata’s Pure Meditation.
It is also called the Samādhi of Single Practice,
and it is also called the Samādhi of True Suchness (Tathatā). This is the root of all samādhis.
If one can practice and cultivate this in every thought-moment,

This is that which has been transmitted from master to disciple within the lineage of the Dharma.

If they do speak them, then all who hear them ought to receive the robe.
Furthermore, there was a master of Chan who asked:
"Bodhidharma transmitted the mind and did not establish written words."
How can you contradict the discourses and scriptural transmissions of your ancestors?
Recently, he further asked:
"Vimalakīrti has already rebuked [the practice of] sitting in silent meditation."
Heze always rebuked those who fixate their minds;
when Caoqi saw someone sitting in the full lotus posture, he would personally strike them with his staff.
Now I ask: [why is this so?]
Every time you offered instruction and admonition, you would urge them to practice seated meditation;
thus, meditation huts were lined up throughout the crags and valleys.
Yet, this deviates from the essential school and contravenes the patriarchs.
I have privately harbored doubts regarding this.
Although I have responded to each person according to the occasion,
those who remain in doubt number in the thousands.
I pity those who have not yet heard [the truth].
Moreover, as for those things they find difficult to accept, their dispositions are all characterized by pervasive attachment,
and these attachments differ from one another.
Since these views contradict one another,
resolving such doubts through debate only exacerbates their existing afflictions; therefore,
it is necessary to clarify the meaning by opening three gates.

I shall evaluate the entire Tripitaka to comprehensively answer the aforementioned doubts, ensuring nothing remains unpenetrated; subsequently, I will provide footnotes for each passage according to its context and meaning,
pointing out how they resolve these various difficulties.
If you wish to see the answers, you must examine the annotations.
Regarding the seven points where the meanings differ and which must be carefully distinguished:
whenever one wishes to clearly understand the nature and characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, [one must rely on these distinctions].
First, one must distinguish the dharma and its meaning;
by interpreting the meaning according to the dharma,
the meaning will become clear.
When phenomena are explained through their meanings,
the phenomena themselves become manifest.
For now, let us clarify this by means of worldly objects.
Just as genuine gold, through conditions such as those of a craftsman, is fashioned into various objects like rings, bracelets, bowls, and cups,
the nature of the gold never changes into copper or iron;
gold itself is the dharma.
"Unchanging while following conditions" is the meaning.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"What thing is unchanging?"
If asked, "What is it that follows conditions?
one should simply answer, "It is gold.
This serves as a metaphor for the principles and meanings of the entire collection of the *Āgama* and *Śāstra*.
It is simply a matter of speaking of the mind.
The mind is itself the Dharma;
everything is its meaning.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The immeasurable meanings arise from a single dharma.
Now, these immeasurable meanings are, in sum, of only two kinds.
First, it is unchanging;
second, it accords with conditions.
The various sutras speak only of this mind following the conditions of delusion or enlightenment to become defiled or pure, ordinary or sage, affliction or bodhi, and out-flowing or non-out-flowing.
It is also simply said that when this mind is defiled or pure, it is fundamentally unchanging, eternally quiescent, and truly suchness (tathatā).
Suppose someone were to ask:
"What dharma do you say is unchanging?"
If one asks which dharma conforms to conditions,
the proper answer is simply "the mind.
That which does not change is the nature (prakṛti).
Following conditions is the characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
One should know that both nature (svabhāva) and characteristic are meanings within the single mind.
As for the fact that the two schools of nature and characteristic now mutually refute one another:
This is truly because one does not recognize the true mind;
whenever the word "mind" (citta) is heard, one assumes it refers merely to the eight consciousnesses.
One fails to realize that the eight consciousnesses are merely the functioning of the true mind in accordance with conditions.
Therefore, Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa took the single mind as the dharma and the two gates of true thusness and arising-and-ceasing as the meaning.
The treatise states:
Based on this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed:
the suchness of the mind is its essence,
while the arising and ceasing of the mind constitutes its characteristics and functions.
It is simply because this mind is not false that it is called "True" (zhen),
and because it does not undergo change or transformation that it is called "Suchness" (ru).
Therefore, throughout the treatise, each instance speaks of "the True Suchness of the Mind" (xinzhenru) and "the Arising and Ceasing of the Mind" (xingshengmie).
In the present age, many practitioners of meditation do not understand its meaning;
thus, they merely refer to the mind as "meditation.
Likewise, many lecturers do not understand the Dharma.
Therefore, one should explain the meaning solely by means of names;
for if one follows the names and gives rise to attachments, it will be difficult to achieve correct understanding.
Those of shallow learning will take what is superficial to be profound.
Alternatively, one may take "nature" (xing) as the phenomenon (fa) and "mind" (xin) as its meaning (yi).

Thus, it is necessary to correlate the three schools with the sūtras and śāstras; once the phenomena and their meanings are clearly revealed, they all converge in the single mind, naturally free from dispute.
Regarding the eight types of mind where the nature, characteristics, and names are identical but the meanings differ:
various sūtras may denounce the mind as a thief,
enjoining its eradication.
Some praise the mind as being the Buddha,
encouraging its cultivation.
Others speak of the virtuous mind and the evil mind, the pure mind and the defiled mind, the mind of greed, the mind of anger, the mind of loving-kindness, and the mind of compassion.
Some say that the mind arises by relying on objects;
some say that the mind arises within objects;
others say that quiescent extinction is the mind.
Some say that the mind consists of objective referents and mental objects;
thus, there are various such contradictions.
If these different schools were not presented in contrast to one another, [the distinctions would remain obscured].
Then how does one who studies the sutras distinguish this?
Is it that there are many kinds of mind,
or is it rather that there is only one general kind of mind?
Now, to briefly indicate the names and essential natures:
generally speaking, there are four types of "mind."
The Sanskrit terms are translated individually and differ as well.
One is *hṛdaya*,
which here means "flesh-heart."
This is the heart among the five viscera within the body, as fully explained in the *Huangting jing* (Scripture of the Yellow Court) and the *Wuzang lun* (Treatise on the Five Viscera).

Second is the mind of discursive thought (*yuanlü xīn*). This refers to the eight consciousnesses, as they are all capable of cognizing their respective objects; thus, visible form is the object of the visual consciousness.
Up to and including the sense faculties, the body, the seeds, and the receptacle world, these are the objects of the ālayavijñāna;

since each perceives only a single portion [of the whole], they are said to be "self-referential" (svabhāga). These eight [consciousnesses] each possess mental factors (caitta) distinguished by being either wholesome or unwholesome.
Within the various sūtras,
all mental factors (caitta) are collectively designated as "mind" (citta),
such as wholesome mind, unwholesome mind, and so forth.
"Trisattva. This refers to the mind that arises as a collection;
it is exclusively the eighth consciousness.

Because the accumulated seeds give rise to active manifestations, the *Nei dan jing* (Yellow Court Scripture) and the *Wu zang lun* (Treatise on the Five Viscera) designate them as "spirits" (*shen*).
This is the view of the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions.
When calculated as "self," these are all this consciousness’s four *kandharidhaya*;
this is translated as the "solid and substantial mind."
It is also called the "mind of true reality" (*zhēnshí xīn*).
This is the true mind (*zhēnxīn*).
However, the eighth consciousness has no separate self-substance (*svabhāva*).
However, because the true mind is characterized by non-awakening,
it possesses the sense of both union and non-union with various deluded thoughts.
As for the sense of union:
That which can contain both defilement and purity is designated as the *ālayavijñāna*;
that which is non-composite and whose essence is eternally unchanging is designated as *tathatā*.
All are the Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus, the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
"That which is quiescent and extinguished is called the One Mind."
The single mind is the Tathāgatagarbha;
the Tathāgatagarbha is also the Dharmakāya in bondage.
As stated in the Śrīmālā-sūtra:
Therefore, one should know that these four kinds of mind are fundamentally of one and the same substance.
Thus, the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* states:

"The Buddha taught that the Tathāgatagarbha, the Dharma-body while enmeshed in bondage, is designated by the name 'Ālayavijñāna. Those of evil wisdom cannot understand that the 'garbha' is none other than the Ālayavijñāna; they falsely hold that True Suchness (Tathatā) and the essence of the Ālaya are distinct entities."
This is the Tathāgata’s pure treasury, the ālaya of the world;
it is like gold and a finger-ring, which are mutually indistinguishable—the finger-ring and other such metaphors illustrate the ālaya.
Gold is used as a metaphor for True Suchness (tathatā).
While it is collectively termed the Tathāgatagarbha, although they share the same substance,
their meanings as "truth" and "delusion" differ, and their aspects as "root" and "branch" are likewise distinct.
The first three are characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and the last one is nature (svabhāva).
There is a specific reason why characteristics arise based on nature;
likewise, there is a specific reason why characteristics are integrated back into nature.
The nature and its characteristics are unimpeded, all being the one mind.
To be deluded by it is to turn one's face toward a wall;
to awaken to it is for the myriad dharmas to appear before a mirror.
If you merely seek the literal meaning of the words or rely on your own subjective convictions,
how will you understand the nature and characteristics of this single mind?
Regarding the ninth point, "Awakening and Cultivation: Sudden and Gradual," which appears paradoxical yet is consistent [with the truth]:
this refers to various sutras, śāstras, and dhyāna manuals that state that one first achieves success through gradual cultivation based on causes.
There is sudden awakening all at once;
some say that one must first achieve sudden awakening before one can engage in gradual cultivation;
others say that through gradual cultivation, one attains gradual awakening.
Some say that both awakening and cultivation are gradual;
some say they are both sudden;
others say that the Dharma has neither sudden nor gradual aspects, for it is the capacity of the practitioner that determines whether it is sudden or gradual.
As stated above, each [point] has its own significance.
Regarding the statement "by way of the opposite":
If it is said that one becomes a Buddha immediately upon awakening and is thus called "sudden" because one originally possesses no afflictions,
then one should not practice the cultivation of abandonment. How,
then, can it be further claimed that there is gradual cultivation?
Gradual cultivation means that afflictions have not yet been exhausted,
causal practices have not yet reached perfection,
and the virtues of fruition have not yet been fulfilled.
What is meant by "sudden"?
The sudden is not the gradual;
the gradual is not the sudden.
Therefore, it is said that they are contrary;
as will be seen in the following comparison,
the sudden and gradual approaches are not merely non-contradictory.
On the contrary, they actually support one another.
Regarding the lineage of transmission from master to disciple, one must recognize the medicine and the illness;
that is to say, the expedient means of the successive transmissions all first reveal the fundamental nature.
I am now directing them to cultivate dhyāna based on their inherent nature (*prakṛti*).
Since this nature is not easily realized and is largely obscured by attachment to signs (*nimitta*),
one must first shatter such attachments in order to reveal that nature.
In the expedient means for shattering attachments, both the ordinary and the sagely must be extinguished together, and both merit and fault must be eliminated equally.
Thus, regarding precepts, there is neither transgression nor observance;
regarding meditation, there is neither concentration nor distraction.
The thirty-two marks are all like flowers in the sky;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are all like dreams and illusions.
This is intended to ensure that the mind remains free from attachment.
Only then can one cultivate dhyāna.
Those of later generations with shallow understanding,
however, take this statement alone as the ultimate path.
Furthermore, because many people are negligent regarding the gateway of cultivation,

[the Buddha] again explains at length the methods of rejoicing and revulsion, the censure of greed and anger, the praise of diligence and frugality, and the sequential stages of training the body, training the breath, and the coarse and subtle [levels of meditation].
Later generations, hearing this, again became confused regarding the function of original enlightenment (mūlapratyavekṣā-jñāna) and consequently adhered exclusively to its phenomenal aspects;
only those with sharp faculties and firm resolve [were able to understand].
Only by serving one's teacher from beginning to end can one attain the essential principles of awakening and cultivation.
Those of a fickle and shallow nature, however,
claim to have reached sufficiency as soon as they hear a single point.
Relying instead on their meager wisdom, they immediately became teachers of others;
failing to exhaustively investigate the fundamental origins and final conclusions, they mostly fell into partial attachments.
Consequently, those following the sudden and gradual gates regarded one another as bitter enemies.
The rivalry between the Northern and Southern Schools was like that between Chu and Han;
their instructions on washing the feet and the parable of the elephant were [no different].
This is verified by this very instance.
As for what is presented here now,
it is certainly not intended to constitute a separate, independent collection to which [the texts] might be brought together.
The endeavor lies in the three dots forming the character "I" (伊).
Since the three dots do not constitute "I" when they are separate,
how can the Three Schools form a Buddha if they are in discord?

Therefore, one who wishes to understand the transmission of the medicine for the disease must see that the three schools do not contradict one another and must comprehend the three types of Buddhist teachings.
Regarding this, someone previously raised an objection as follows:
"How can you, O Chan Master, engage in such lecturing?
I now answer this entirely with these ten points.
Thus, at the outset, I have already stated that the patriarchs of the Western Regions all propagated the sūtras and śāstras.
